task: get a car-insurance quote online and proceed toward buying the policy: enter vehicle and driver details, choose coverage options and deductibles, review the quote price, and continue toward purchase; complete when a priced quote (or a purchase confirmation) is on screen. Surface pinned: an insurer's quote website or app (GEICO, Progressive, State Farm, Allstate, Root). Variants: insurance-agent sales training, "cheapest insurance" talking-head advice, and claims filing do not belong.

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step requires sharing your highly sensitive Social Security Number with the agent, which poses a significant privacy and security risk.
questions.check: Does the form ask for a Social Security number, for the applicant or any household member, is the field marked optional or recommended, and what does the page say it is used for?
questions.say_example: The form asks for your Social Security number. It says it's optional, for a more accurate price. I never hold that number. Type it in yourself, or say skip.

questions.question: What type of driving license do you hold?
questions.why: The type of driving license you hold, such as an international license, is a major factor in determining your insurance quote.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might guess your license type incorrectly, which could lead to an inaccurate quote or an invalid policy.
questions.check: Which licence type is selected, and which options does the form offer?
questions.say_example: Set licence type to <full US licence>.

questions.question: Does the licence date entered agree with how long the form says you've held it?
questions.why: You selected 'Less than 1 Year' for your license duration but entered an acquisition date of February 20, 2022, creating a contradiction that could invalidate your quote.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the guarantee of an accurate quote because contradictory driver history details can lead to incorrect pricing or a rejected policy.
questions.check: What licence-held duration is selected, and what licence date is entered? Do they agree with each other and with today's date?
questions.say_example: The form says you've held your licence under a year, but the date entered is <February 2022>. Those don't match. Fixing the duration. Otherwise the quote can be thrown out.

questions.question: When did you first obtain your driver's license?
questions.why: The form requires the month and year you first obtained your license in the U.S. or Canada to accurately assess your driving history.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might guess your licensing date, which could result in an inaccurate insurance quote or an invalid policy.
questions.check: What licence start or first-obtained month and year is entered?
questions.say_example: Entered the licence date as <June 2015>.

questions.question: The form asks for your driving licence number and offers a box to say you can't or won't give it. Do you give it, or tick the box?
questions.why: The form requests your exact driving licence number but provides a checkbox to explicitly state you cannot or do not want to provide it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to legally bypass this field, risking a halted process or an invalid policy if the agent enters a fake number instead of using the provided opt-out.
questions.check: Does the form ask for a driving licence number, and is there a checkbox to say the applicant cannot or does not want to provide it?
questions.say_example: It wants your driving licence number. There's a box to say you'd rather not give it. Read me the number, or say leave it out.

questions.question: Do you need to report any accidents, tickets, or other incidents on your driving record?
questions.why: The screen asks if any drivers have had accidents, traffic tickets, DUIs, or license suspensions within the last 5 to 10 years.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might fail to report your past driving incidents, resulting in an inaccurate quote or future coverage issues.
questions.check: Does the page ask about accidents, tickets, claims, DUIs or suspensions over a stated number of years, is No pre-selected, and for which drivers?
questions.say_example: The form already ticked No for accidents and tickets in the last <5> years. Is that true? I'll only keep it if you say so.

questions.question: Are your pre-filled driver's license details correct?
questions.why: The screen showed a pre-filled Florida driver's license ending in [account number], which must be accurate to ensure a valid insurance quote.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify that their current and correct driver's license number is being used for the quote.
questions.check: What licence state and last digits does the page show pre-filled, and do they match the licence in the task or profile?
questions.say_example: The site pre-filled a <Florida> licence ending <[account number]>. Yours is <California>. Fixing it.

questions.question: The site couldn't pull your credit. Do you want to lift a credit freeze first, or carry on without it?
questions.why: Many users keep their credit frozen, which blocks the insurer's soft pull for an insurance score, often resulting in a default to the highest possible pricing tier or a hard stop.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might proceed with a heavily penalized 'no-hit' credit tier quote instead of pausing so the user can temporarily lift their credit freeze for a better rate.
questions.check: Does the page say it could not obtain a credit history or report, and does it offer to continue without it?
questions.say_example: The site couldn't pull your credit, so it may price you as if it were poor. If you've got a credit freeze on, you could lift it and I'll retry. Lift it, or carry on without?

questions.question: Does the insurer's record show an accident or ticket you didn't mention?
questions.why: Insurers run background checks (like CLUE or MVR) and will halt the quote or spike the price if they find unreported incidents, sometimes requiring you to dispute them if they belong to someone else.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to dispute an incorrect driving record pulled by the system, potentially accepting a drastically inflated premium for an accident that wasn't yours.
questions.check: Does the page list any accident, ticket or claim pulled from a record, and does the task or an earlier answer declare it?
questions.say_example: The insurer's record shows a <speeding ticket in 2024> you didn't mention. If it's not yours you can dispute it. Is it yours?

questions.question: What does the site need to know about your spouse?

questions.check: Which fields does the page require for the added driver, and which are filled?
questions.say_example: Filled in <[name]>'s details as the second driver.

questions.question: Did the site find people at your address and add them as drivers?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to catch and exclude auto-discovered drivers, which could result in them being silently added to your policy and inflating your rate.
questions.check: Does the page show household members it found from records, in a popup or sidebar, and are they marked to be added unless excluded?
questions.say_example: The site found <two> people it thinks live with you, <[name]> and <[name]>. They'll be added as drivers unless I exclude them. Do they drive your car?

questions.question: Have you lived at your current address for less than two years?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might guess your household vehicle count or access to other cars, potentially causing you to miss out on discounts or invalidating your policy with incorrect information.
questions.check: What number of household cars is entered, what is answered about access to other vehicles, and what is answered about children under 16 living at the address?

questions.question: Are you in any group, like the military or an employer, that gets a discount?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You could miss out on a lower insurance premium if the agent skips selecting an organization you actually belong to.
questions.check: Which affiliation or membership discounts does the page offer, and which are selected?
questions.say_example: Said no to military, government and group discounts. You didn't mention one. One would cut the price.

questions.check: Does the page ask who owns the car, which options does it offer, and what is selected?

questions.question: Should the car's owner be allowed to renew or change the policy?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this decision means the agent might incorrectly grant or withhold policy management permissions for the car owner.
questions.check: Does the page ask whether the car owner may renew or amend the policy, and what is selected?

questions.question: What contact details does the site need to show prices?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to strategically use a dummy phone number to avoid spam calls while ensuring the name exactly matches your vehicle registration.
questions.check: Which contact fields does the page require to show prices, and does it ask about marketing or contact preferences?
questions.say_example: To show prices it wants your name, email, and mobile. I'm filling those in, and saying no to sales calls.

questions.question: What's the right email, since the site says the one typed in isn't valid?

questions.question: Do you want the driving-tracking program for a discount?
questions.why: The screen offers a program that lowers your rate immediately but personalizes it over time based on driving habits tracked via an app or device, which requires evaluating if your actual driving style will benefit you.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might enroll you to get the immediate discount, unknowingly subjecting you to tracking that could increase your rate if you struggle to maintain strict driving habits like following the speed limit.
questions.check: Does the page offer a telematics, tracking or safe-driving program, is it pre-enrolled, and what does it say about the discount and what it tracks?

questions.question: There's a captcha. If my try fails, will you enter it?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to review the specific terms of the inquiry agreement before legally consenting to it.

questions.check: What car value, usage class and payment frequency does the summary show, and do they match what was entered earlier in this run?

questions.check: What start date is selected for the bundled home policy?

questions.check: What current property-insurance status is selected?

questions.question: The quote is over your budget. Which cover do you want to change first to bring it down?
questions.why: The screen lists individual policy coverages with their costs and edit buttons, requiring a choice on which specific protection to modify to reach your target price.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide which specific coverages to reduce based on your personal risk tolerance and budget.
questions.check: What is the quoted total, what budget does the task give, and which itemized coverages carry the largest costs?
questions.say_example: It's <$140> a month, over your <$100>. The biggest piece is collision at <$45>. Drop it, raise the deductible, or keep it and pay more?

questions.question: Does this cover meet what your lender or lease requires?
questions.why: If you finance or lease the car, the lienholder typically requires higher liability limits and lower deductibles than the state minimums the agent might select to get the cheapest price.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure your policy complies with your loan agreement, risking forced-placed insurance by your lender at a much higher cost.
questions.check: Does the page show the car as financed or leased, and does the selected plan include collision and comprehensive? What limits are selected? Does the page offer loan or lease payoff cover, and is it selected?
questions.say_example: Your car has a loan on it. The cheapest plan has no collision cover, and lenders normally require it. I'm keeping collision in. OK?

questions.question: Which plan type do you want, third party or comprehensive?
questions.why: The screen requires you to choose between comprehensive package plans and third-party plans to establish your baseline coverage.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether you need the extensive protection of a comprehensive plan or just basic third-party coverage.
questions.check: Does the page offer comprehensive and third-party plan types, and which is selected?
questions.say_example: Two kinds of plan. <Third party> at <₹2,900> only pays for damage you do to others. <Comprehensive> at <₹8,200> covers your car too. Which one?

questions.question: Which plan do you want, Basic, Standard, or Premium?
questions.why: The screen presents three distinct pricing tiers with different monthly costs and liability limits to choose from.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally weigh the financial trade-offs between budget-friendly monthly premiums and higher liability protection limits.
questions.check: Which coverage tiers does the page offer, and for each, what is the price per month or term, the bodily injury and property damage limits, and which of collision, comprehensive and uninsured motorist are included or missing?
questions.say_example: Three plans. <Basic> is <$192> a month, <$50,000> per person for injuries, and no cover for your own car. <Standard> is <$230> with <$100,000> and your car covered. <Premium> is <$317>. Which one? Say Basic, Standard, or Premium.

questions.question: Do you want me to read what any of the coverages means?
questions.why: The screen provides detailed explanations of what specific coverages pay for, such as medical or funeral expenses regardless of fault.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally understand the exact protections, limits, and benefits included in your insurance policy.
questions.check: For each coverage line, what explanation does the tooltip or info panel give?
questions.say_example: Ask me what any of these covers means and I'll read you the site's explanation.

questions.question: What should the car's insured value, the IDV, be set to?
questions.why: The screen provides a slider to customize your IDV, which dictates the maximum payout from the insurer in the event of total damage or theft.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent decide means you lose control over balancing your premium costs against the potential payout for a total loss.
questions.check: What Insured Declared Value is set, what range does the slider allow, and how does the premium change across it?
questions.say_example: The site set your car's insured value at <₹11,40,000>. That's the most it'd pay if the car's written off. Higher costs more each year. Keep it?

questions.question: Which deductible do you want, given how much it changes the premium?
questions.why: The screen displays how different deductible levels directly change your 6-month premium, requiring a trade-off between upfront costs and out-of-pocket risk for non-collision damage.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means losing the opportunity to align the deductible with your personal risk tolerance and financial preference for lower premiums versus lower repair costs.
questions.check: Which deductible or excess options does the page offer, for which coverage, and how does the premium change for each?
questions.say_example: A <$500> deductible is <$40> more per six months than <$1,000>. Which do you want to pay if you have a crash, <500> or <1,000>?

questions.question: Which recommended add-ons do you want to include in your policy?
questions.why: The screen presents optional coverages like Zero Depreciation and Roadside Assistance that provide extra protection for specific scenarios.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to weigh the value of specific extra protections against their additional cost based on your personal driving needs.
questions.check: Which optional add-ons does the page offer, at what price each, and which are selected? Does selecting one change the quoted premium?
questions.say_example: It's offering extras. <Zero depreciation> for <₹1,200>, <roadside help> for <₹150>, <key cover> for <₹90>. Want any? Say none, or name them.

questions.question: Does the car have fitted extras to declare?
questions.why: The screen provides optional checkboxes to declare the value of additionally-fitted electrical and non-electrical accessories so they are included in the policy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might not declare your aftermarket additions, leaving expensive upgrades like custom stereos or alloy wheels unprotected in a claim.
questions.check: Does the page ask for the value of fitted accessories, electrical or otherwise, and is anything entered?
questions.say_example: It asks whether the car has fitted extras, like a stereo or a CNG kit, to cover. You didn't mention any, so I'm leaving it blank. Say so if there are.

questions.question: Before the add-ons get cleared, are there any of the checked ones you want to keep?
questions.why: The sidebar displays a 'Clear all' button alongside 11 individually checked add-on boxes, offering a choice between a single click and multiple manual clicks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to save time by using the 'Clear all' button or to manually review and uncheck each add-on individually.
questions.check: How many add-on boxes are pre-checked, what are they, and is there a Clear all control?

questions.question: Do you want the no-fault option, which limits your right to sue?

questions.check: Does the page offer a no-fault or limited-tort option, and what does its tooltip say about the right to sue?
questions.say_example: There's a <no fault> option that lowers the price. It means you mostly can't sue the other driver after a crash. Add it, or leave it?

questions.question: How many days of cover do you need?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to balance the upfront total cost against the per-day value based on their personal timeline and budget.
questions.check: Which policy durations does the page offer, and what is the total and per-day cost of each?
questions.say_example: Cover runs from <30> to <180> days. <90> days is <£150>, about <£1.67> a day. How long do you need it?

questions.say_example: Here's the quote. <$640> for six months, or <$107> a month. <$100,000> per person for injuries, <$50,000> for damage, <$1,000> deductibles.

questions.question: Is there a star or footnote mark next to the big price?
questions.why: Insurers often display the monthly premium in huge text while hiding installment fees, down payment requirements, or conditions behind an asterisk in a much smaller, lighter font.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to spot visually downplayed conditions, potentially agreeing to a policy where the actual cost is higher than the boldly advertised number.
questions.check: Is there an asterisk, dagger or footnote marker beside the headline premium, and what does the footnote text say?
questions.say_example: The big <$107> a month has a star next to it. The small print says that's after a <$300> down payment first.

questions.question: Are the quote and your current bill priced for the same period?
questions.why: The screen defaults to showing monthly rates for the different coverage tiers, but you can switch to a six-month view to accurately compare the quote against your current policy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might just accept the default monthly view, depriving you of a direct six-month price comparison that matches how you currently budget for insurance.
questions.check: Is the displayed price per month or per term, does a toggle exist, and which period does the task's current-policy figure use?
questions.say_example: This quote shows a monthly rate. Your current bill is per six months, so I'm switching the view before comparing.

questions.question: Do you want to pay in full upfront to get the discount, or choose the monthly payment plan?
questions.why: The screen shows a specific discount for paying in full upfront compared to the total cost of the monthly payment plan.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to balance your immediate cash flow needs against the total savings of paying the policy in full.
questions.check: Which payment plans does the page offer, what is due today and monthly for each, and what is the total of each plan?
questions.say_example: Paying all <$844> now saves <$194>. The monthly plan is <$173> a month and comes to <$1,038>. Pay in full, or monthly?

questions.question: Are there enough authorized cashless garages in your area?
questions.why: The modal showed a list of 116 authorized dealer garages in Delhi, which confirms whether you will have convenient repair options if you need to file a claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify if your preferred local repair shops are included in the insurer's cashless network.
questions.check: How many cashless or network garages does the page list for the area, and how many for the other plans shown?
questions.say_example: This plan has <zero> cashless garages near you. You'd pay for repairs up front and claim the money back. <HDFC> has <116> nearby. Still this one?

questions.question: Are these prices still estimates that will change once the car and drivers are in?
questions.why: The screen displays preliminary quotes starting at $14 per month, but the progress bar shows the profile is only 69% complete.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to observe how your driver details alone influence the preliminary rates before adding your vehicle.
questions.check: Does the page show preliminary or estimated prices alongside a progress indicator, and what percentage complete does it show?
questions.say_example: These prices are only <69%> done. They'll change once the car and drivers are in. I'm carrying on until they're final.

questions.question: Has the price finished updating after the change?
questions.why: Adjusting deductibles or limits often triggers an asynchronous price recalculation where the premium text temporarily grays out or shows a spinner before displaying the new cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If the agent scrapes the price too quickly, you might be quoted the old premium, leading to unexpected costs when you actually purchase the policy.
questions.check: After a coverage change, is the premium greyed out or showing a spinner, or has a new value settled?
questions.say_example: Waited for the price to finish updating before reading it.

questions.question: Do the quote's limits and deductibles match your current policy's?
questions.why: Verifying that the quote's $50,000/$100,000 limits match the paper document ensures you are getting an accurate price comparison for the same level of coverage.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the assurance that the new quote provides the exact same level of liability protection as your existing policy.
questions.check: What bodily injury, property damage, uninsured motorist and personal injury limits, what deductibles, and which extra lines such as rental or roadside does the quote show, and what does the task give for the current policy? Which lines differ?
questions.say_example: The quote has <$25,000> per person for injuries. Your current policy has <$50,000>. That's less protection, so it's not a like-for-like price. Raise it to match, or keep the cheaper cover?

questions.question: What do you pay now, for the same term?
questions.why: Establishing your current premium provides a necessary financial benchmark to evaluate whether the new quote is actually a better deal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to factor in their personal, offline financial baseline to decide if the new quote is competitive enough to purchase.
questions.check: What current premium and term does the task give as the baseline?
questions.say_example: Took your current <$780> for six months as the baseline.

questions.question: How much will you save over six months compared to your current policy?
questions.why: Comparing the $640.00 six-month quote on the screen to your handwritten notes helps you determine if switching policies is financially worthwhile.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify the exact savings against your offline records before committing to the new policy.
questions.check: What is the quoted total for the term, and what current premium for the same term does the task give? What is the difference?
questions.say_example: This quote is <$640> for six months. You're paying <$780> now, so that's <$140> less for the same cover.

questions.question: Does the final quote work out to the advertised daily rate?
questions.why: The final 180-day quote of £292.60 shown on screen contradicts both the narrator's estimate and the £1.23 daily rate displayed earlier.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to notice the misleading pricing and reject a quote that is significantly higher than expected.
questions.check: What headline or 'from' daily rate did the product page advertise, and what total and duration does the final quote show? What is the quoted total divided by the days?
questions.say_example: The page advertised from <£1.23> a day. The <180>-day quote is <£292.60>, which is <£1.63> a day. The 'from' price isn't what you'd pay.

questions.question: Do the itemized coverage costs match the savings shown when you try to remove them?
questions.why: The itemized list priced roadside assistance at $5, but the edit screen stated removing it saves $26.89, revealing a significant pricing discrepancy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to catch contradictory pricing information that might change which optional coverages you decide to buy.
questions.check: What price does the itemized list give for a coverage, and what saving does the edit or remove screen state for taking it off? Do they agree?
questions.say_example: Roadside shows as <$5> on the list, but removing it says it saves <$26.89>. The list isn't telling the whole price.

questions.question: Do the itemized coverages and fees add up to the total quoted price?
questions.why: Verifying that the itemized coverages for the [address] Rogue and the associated fees equal the final quoted price ensures there are no hidden costs or discrepancies.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally audit the quote's math to ensure the itemized costs accurately reflect the final pay-in-full price.
questions.check: What itemized coverage costs and fees does the quote list, and what total does it show? Does the sum equal the total?
questions.say_example: The lines on the quote add up to <$612>, but the total says <$640>. There's <$28> in there the list doesn't show.

questions.question: Do the deposit and installments add up to the quoted total, and does each match the advertised monthly amount?
questions.why: The payment screen warns that monthly installments typically incur interest, so checking the math confirms whether you are actually being charged extra.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify if the monthly payment plan is effectively a zero-percent interest offer despite the warning.
questions.check: What deposit and installments does the payment schedule list, what is the advertised monthly amount, and what is the quoted total? Do the installments match the advertised figure, and does the sum equal the total?
questions.say_example: The schedule adds up to <$1,038>. The quote said <$844>. That's <$194> of interest and fees for paying monthly.

questions.question: Do the discount amounts shown on the quote agree with each other and with the payment schedule?
questions.why: The 'Discount Savings' box stated $237.00 in savings, but a banner below claimed $350.00 in discounts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might ignore the conflicting discount amounts, leaving you uncertain about the actual savings applied to your policy.
questions.check: What discount or credit amounts does the page state, in the savings box, any banner, and the payment schedule? Do they agree?
questions.say_example: The savings box says <$237> in discounts. A banner just below says <$350>. One of those isn't real, so I'm going by the schedule.

questions.question: Which insurer do you want?
questions.why: The screen displays 10 different plans based on your ₹11,40,000 IDV, requiring you to weigh premium prices against metrics like claim settlement rates.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally evaluate the trade-offs between premium costs and insurer reliability to find the best fit for your budget.
questions.check: Which insurers or plans does the results page list, and for each, what premium, insured value, claim settlement ratio and cover type does it show?
questions.say_example: Two that fit. <HDFC ERGO> at <₹3,863>, insured value <₹11,40,000>, <98%> of claims paid. <Bajaj> at <₹4,400>, same value, <96%>. Which one? Say HDFC or Bajaj.

questions.question: When should the cover start?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the awareness that the funds will be deducted from your account immediately, which could impact your current cash flow or cause overdrafts if you expected the charge to align with the future start date.
questions.check: Does the page say the payment method will be charged today regardless of the start date?
questions.say_example: One thing. Even with a start date of <the 15th>, it charges your card today. OK?

questions.question: Are the vehicle details, plan summary, and final premium correct before you pay?

questions.check: What vehicle, plan type, cover, and total does the pay screen show, and do they match the plan and car selected earlier in this run?

questions.question: Are the pre-filled contact and bank details yours?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: A person delegating this task loses the chance to verify or correct their personal contact and payment information before finalizing the purchase.
questions.check: What email, phone and bank account or IBAN does the checkout show pre-filled, and do they match the task or profile?
questions.say_example: The pay page has an account ending <[account number]> pre-filled. That's not the one you gave me. Fixing it before anything's charged.

questions.question: Does the base premium on the final summary match the quote you selected on the results page?
questions.why: Confirming that the base premium remains consistent between the results and summary pages ensures no hidden fees were added before the final taxes were applied.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to verify that the final price is calculated correctly from the original quote without unexpected base rate changes.
questions.check: What premium did the selected quote show on the results page, and what base premium does the summary or checkout show? Do they match?
questions.say_example: The price was <$640> when you picked it. The checkout now says <$712>. That usually means the insurer just ran your driving record. Stopping so you can see it before it's paid.

questions.question: Does the checkout total equal the listed premium plus tax, less any discount shown?
questions.why: Verifying that the ₹3,415 premium and ₹615 GST equal the ₹4,030 final charge ensures no hidden fees were added before payment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify the final math yourself and ensure you aren't being overcharged at checkout.
questions.check: What premium, tax and any discount does the checkout list, and what total does it show? Is there a collapsed taxes, fees or breakdown section near the total, and when expanded, what does it list? Does premium plus tax minus discount plus those fees equal the total?

questions.question: Does the No Claim Bonus percentage on the proposal form match what you selected on the quotes page?

questions.check: What No Claim Bonus percentage does the proposal form show, and what did the quotes page show?
questions.say_example: The quotes page had your no-claims bonus at <35%>. The proposal form now says <45%>. Fixing it, or the policy's built on a bonus you don't have.

questions.question: Is the optional marketing opt-in left unticked?

questions.check: Does the page offer a marketing opt-in, prize draw or similar, and is it left unticked?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to halt the process before committing your final contact details and payment information.
questions.check: Which required contact field, phone or email, is the page blocked on, and does the task or profile supply a value for it?
questions.say_example: It won't go on without a phone number, and I don't have one for you. What number should I put?

questions.question: Do you want your policy documents by email or by post?
questions.why: The screen provides checkboxes for paperless billing, electronic policy documents, and text alerts, which dictate how the insurer will deliver your information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose whether you receive physical mail or digital copies for your insurance bills and ID cards.
questions.check: Which delivery options does the page offer, paperless, electronic documents, text alerts, and which are selected? Does it state a price difference?
questions.say_example: Chose paperless documents. It's <$8> cheaper.

questions.question: Do you require an SR-22 certificate of financial responsibility?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If the agent incorrectly assumes you do not need an SR-22, you could receive an invalid quote or fail to meet your state's legal driving requirements.
questions.check: Does the page ask whether any driver needs an SR-22 or certificate of financial responsibility, and what is answered?
questions.say_example: Said no to needing an SR-22.

questions.question: Are the things the site asks you to confirm all true?
questions.why: Blindly agreeing to the confirmation statements risks invalidating your coverage if your circumstances do not match the specific conditions listed on the screen, such as the policy ending once you pass your driving test.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify that their personal situation actually complies with the strict legal and eligibility criteria required for the insurance policy to be valid.
questions.check: Which confirmation statements, eligibility rules or terms does the page require agreeing to before purchase, and what does each say?

questions.question: Is it OK for the insurer to send automated calls and texts?

questions.check: Is there a checkbox consenting to automated or prerecorded calls and texts, is it required, and is it left unticked?

questions.check: Does the page show a previous balance or outstanding amount that must be paid before the policy is issued, and how much?
